item.title: An updated Clairic and Clairic-flash are now open-weight, from the new Workers AI Superintelligence team
item.description: Clairic graduates from preview, while Clairic-flash joins the repertoire on Workers AI. We’re doing an open-weight release for both extraction models.
item.dc:creator: Alex Reneau
Michelle Chen
Kevin Flansburg
item.content:encoded:
Cloudflare has become a neolab. We’re building our own frontier AI models for our customers and the open-source community.

Today, we’re announcing two open-weight model releases:

  • We’re introducing an updated version of Clairic. Since the preview, we’ve improved extraction from complex documents including images and PDFs (new!), with more reliable handling of tables, lists, and dates, and better grounding of answers in the source material.
  • We’re introducing Clairic-flash, a lighter, faster version of Clairic that delivers strong extraction and prediction performance in a compact, 9-billion-parameter model.

Both extraction models are hosted on Workers AI and full open weights are available on Hugging Face.

We’re also excited to re-introduce ourselves as the Workers AI superintelligence team, the frontier AI research team behind Clef, Clairic, and lots more in the works. This team is working quickly to push the AI frontier and build useful models for Cloudflare’s customers and the open source community.

A new version of Clairic: redesigned after the preview release

Since announcing Clairic in preview, we have received a ton of use cases and helpful feedback on how customers wanted to use an extraction model. We heard about use cases ranging from extracting data from images like receipts to reading values from support tickets. We knew that we wanted extraction to be the clear focus for the model, so it had to excel at reading from unstructured data.

We decided to go back to the drawing board with Clairic and redesigned our architecture, differentiating this new version of Clairic from our preview release. For ordinary text and number extraction fields, we now use parallel slot autoregressive generation instead of a single forward pass. Each field uses the tokens it has already written to choose its next token, then stops at its own end marker. All the fields advance together in the serving batch, still giving lightning-fast latency per request. This boosted our accuracy in extraction for both text and images, and the trade-off in accuracy offsets the small latency cost. For computation, estimation, and extraction use cases, we trained special heads that can handle estimates, forecasts, durations, calculated dates, and explicit arithmetic.

Although the model architecture evolved, we kept the parts of the typed API interface that make the answers useful: confidence scores, character spans, and probabilities are still intact with every request. The model is still incredibly fast and cheap. From the evals below, you can see how our newer versions of Clairic have greatly improved on extraction across text, images, PDFs, and more.

There are no public extraction benchmarks yet, but we ran our internal evals for other emerging extraction models on the market, such as Liquid AI’s D1.2 (pipelined with Apple Vision for optical character recognition) and Scaledown’s Extract. Our Clairic models excel across extraction use cases, but take these evals as directional guidance since they are self-reported. We wanted to show an illustrative picture of how Clairic is performing across generalized extraction use cases and celebrate the fact that other companies are releasing extraction models as well — confirming our original hypothesis that extraction was a pain point for LLM users because of the cost, latency, and accuracy.

But is it fast?

We ran latency tests for Clairic and Clairic-flash, measuring complete HTTP response from a self-hosted server, including all fields in the request. Even with the redesigned architecture, you can expect responses in under one second — much faster than typical LLM responses for similar workloads.

Better extraction for images and PDFs

In our preview blog post, Clairic read a photo of a receipt. Now the Clairic family of models can read PDFs too, so you can ask for the supplier, line items, and total in one request, even when they appear on different pages. You can include up to four images or PDF pages in total, and line items can come back as rows that keep each description, quantity, and price together. Due to Clairic’s new architecture, image reading accuracy has improved from 207 errors to 0 on our internal benchmarks, explicitly covering text and images.

Promotional pricing on Clairic for a limited time

When we first launched our preview endpoint of Clairic at @cf/cloudflare/clairic, we hosted the 9B variant as it was faster and easier to train, at the preview price of $0.10 per M input tokens. We’re now moving the 9B model to the @cf/cloudflare/clairic-flash endpoint and the 27B model will live at @cf/cloudflare/clairic.

The 27B Clairic model will be priced at $0.24 per M input tokens, while the 9B Clairic-flash model will be priced at $0.10 per M input tokens. Although the model does technically generate output tokens, we decided to keep the System One pricing principles and are only charging on input tokens: we eat the cost of the output token generation.

In order to make this a seamless swap, we’re offering a promotional discount on Clairic — until December 1, 2026, both Clairic and Clairic-flash will cost $0.10 per M input tokens. This means you get to try out the higher quality variant of Clairic at the same price. If your applications are hooked up to the Clairic endpoint that we released in preview, you will automatically benefit from the better extraction capabilities of our new model, which we’re rolling out in place.

If you’d like to move more cost-sensitive workloads to the cheaper 9B Clairic-flash variant, we encourage you to do so. On December 1, we’ll be ending the promotional discount for Clairic and pricing will resume at $0.24 per M input tokens instead of the discounted $0.10 per M input tokens.

Clairic and Clairic-flash (new) are open-weight

Both Clairic models are now open-weight on Hugging Face as well. We have seen an outpouring of experiments and tuned models from our release of Clef, and we’re happy to continue supporting teams and research with our open-weight release of Clairic.

Our mission with these System One models is to help people augment their expensive LLM usage with smaller, faster, cheaper models that are purpose-built for a specific task. We hope that releasing these models open-weight encourages others to experiment and build on our ideas as well.

Try them out

Clairic and Clairic-flash are available on Workers AI as @cf/cloudflare/clairic and @cf/cloudflare/clairic-flash. The developer documentation has the full API schemas, which remain unchanged from our preview endpoint. We’re also publishing the open-weight releases for Clairic and Clairic-flash on Hugging Face. 

The team behind these models — the Workers AI superintelligence team — is just getting started, and growing fast to push frontier AI research at Cloudflare. Join us early and help shape what the superintelligence team becomes.

item.title: Cross-request KV cache exposure in the GLM-5.3 Workers AI model, and our remediation with SGLang
item.description: A configuration mismatch in GLM 5.3 on Workers AI triggered an SGLang bug that exposed KV cache pages across requests. Here is how we addressed the issue.
item.dc:creator: Kevin Flansburg
Michelle Chen
item.content:encoded:
On September 8, 2026, we were alerted by a security researcher, Gadi Evron from Knostic, to a tenant isolation issue affecting the GLM-5.3 Workers AI model (@cf/zai-org/glm-5.3) starting on August 27, 2026. We have remediated the issue, and we restored the model on September 9. We have confirmed that no other model hosted on Workers AI was affected.

Between August 27 and September 9, a small number of customers using the GLM 5.3 Workers AI model received responses that contained data from other customers' requests made to the same model shortly before theirs. In total, 155 responses were affected, all to prompts longer than 681,280 tokens.

After excluding our own testing and the researcher's, the requests we identified are consistent in timing and volume with ordinary long-context use, not with someone repeatedly exploiting the bug. We found no evidence of deliberate exploitation.

Today we are publishing this report alongside a post from SGLang, the open-source inference engine that we use, as a coordinated disclosure. This post describes the bug that caused this issue, our response timeline, and the subsequent hardening we have conducted on our production SGLang deployments. We also detail our continued efforts with the upstream maintainers of SGLang to address this and similar bugs.

What happened

GLM is a text generation model from Z.ai that is built for agentic coding workflows; it is one of the many models available through Workers AI. Gadi Evron submitted a report on September 8 through our HackerOne program stating that very long prompts sent to @cf/zai-org/glm-5.3 on Workers AI sometimes returned text that belonged to other users' sessions. Cloudflare reproduced the issue the next morning and took the model offline within 40 minutes of declaring an incident. We then deployed a corrected configuration and a patched inference engine, and restored service the same day.  

This specific report of cross-request KV cache exposure was the result of two overlapping issues. The first was a misconfiguration of the open-source inference engine, SGLang, used by Cloudflare. We deployed GLM 5.3 with a 1,048,576-token context window, but the KV cache pool on our prefill GPUs only had room for 681,280 tokens. We were aware of this mismatch before launch. We expected the engine to return an error for any prompt it could not process, and our long-context tests returned successful responses, so we did not believe this to be an issue.

The second was a bug in how SGLang handled the resulting over-length requests in disaggregated prefill/decode mode. A prompt that did not fit the pool was internally marked as rejected and replaced with a one-token placeholder, but instead of aborting the request and returning a client error, prefill generated the KV cache for the placeholder prompt and transferred it to the decode node. The decode node received a "transfer complete" message and assumed that prefill overwrote the KV cache from previous requests with the full prompt for this request, when in fact it left the majority of the previous state intact. The decode node subsequently generated a response while attending over stale cache pages that still held data from earlier requests. As a result, responses to prompts longer than 681,280 tokens could contain data from other users' GLM 5.3 sessions.

Immediate remediation

After disabling the model, we took the following actions to correct this vulnerability before restoring public access to it:

To fix our configuration, we made the pool hold the full context. We adjusted our GLM 5.3 configuration to match our GLM 5.2 configuration, which freed enough GPU memory that the prefill KV pool now holds about 2.04 million tokens, roughly twice the 1,048,576-token context length. A prompt that fits the context window now always fits the pool, so the rejection path is never reached for a valid request. This alone prevents the bug from being exercised.

To fix the engine, we also made the rejection path safe. Relying on pool size alone is fragile: any change to quantization, tensor parallelism, CUDA graph sizes, or a future model version changes the pool size in a way that's easy to miss. Furthermore, there may be other situations in which the prefill scheduler can reject a request and trigger the same bug. To prevent this, we also patched the engine so that a request carrying a pending rejection is retired at the disaggregation admission queue, with its original error, before any bootstrap, allocation, or KV transfer happens. We proposed this upstream as #38704, which also had the decode node verify that the number of tokens transferred matches the number it reserved. The fix was already on SGLang main in #36988, merged September 6 for a related failure path but not yet released. The maintainers also merged #38935, which rejects these requests earlier, following our approach.

We validated both changes against the researcher's reproduction script and our own canary-marker tests before restoring the model.

Background: how we serve GLM 5.3

Workers AI runs GLM 5.3 with SGLang in a disaggregated configuration: a pool of prefill GPUs processes the prompt and produces the model's KV cache for it, then hands that cache over remote direct memory access (RDMA), via Mooncake, to a pool of decode GPUs that generate the response. We have written about this architecture before in our posts on high-performance LLMs and smaller, faster, safer models.

The KV cache in GPU memory is a shared pool of fixed-size pages. Each request is assigned pages when it is admitted and releases them when it finishes. Pages are not currently zeroed between requests; the next request that gets a page simply overwrites it. This approach is common among inference engines and is necessary to achieve the best performance, but it means that the inference engine is responsible for tracking ownership of these memory pages. KV cache page ownership and lifetime tracking has to deal with not just shared ownership within a node (KV cache offload and token generation both access the memory with different lifetimes), but also ownership that is technically shared with the remote prefill node (which holds a simultaneous mutable reference to the page).

Furthermore, the size of this pool is not a configuration value. SGLang sizes it at startup from whatever GPU memory remains after loading the model weights. The model's advertised context length is a separate configuration value. Nothing forces the two to agree, and it is our job to check that they do.

Issue one: misconfiguration

On our GLM 5.3 prefill nodes with our configuration, the pool came to 681,280 tokens while the model's context length is 1,048,576 tokens. The selected KV pool size is printed by SGLang in logs during startup and exposed as a metric. We were aware of this size mismatch; however, during pre-launch testing we observed successful HTTP status codes and a streaming body with no error frames during benchmarking. We assumed that the engine was capable of gracefully handling the difference between the KV cache pool and requested context window via streaming or some other mechanism.

This was one critical gap in our testing: we only validated HTTP response codes and engine performance at long contexts, without validating model output and coherence. We now check KV pool size against context length directly, from the running engine, before any disaggregated deployment change ships, rather than inferring it from response codes.

Issue two: SGLang bug

In v0.5.21, the SGLang team has now addressed this bug in how it was handling prompts longer than the KV pool size. Here’s what was happening before.

When a prompt arrived that was longer than the KV pool could hold, SGLang's scheduler rejected it. The rejection path (Req.set_finish_with_abort) recorded the error to be returned to the client and swapped the prompt for a one-token placeholder so that the request could drain through the normal batch machinery without allocating real memory. On a single-node deployment this worked: the placeholder ran, the batch finished, and the client received an error.

In disaggregated mode such as we operate, the admission queues on both prefill and decode checked whether a request was finished, not whether it was rejected. A rejected request reported itself as live. So:

  1. Bootstrap. The router told the decode node the prompt length (8 pages in the diagram). Decode reserved 8 KV pages for the request.
  2. Prefill admission. The prefill admission queue admitted any request where req.finished() was False. A rejected request stored its rejection in to_finish, not finished_reason, so finished() still returned False. The rejected request was admitted.
  3. Prefill forward pass. Rejection had already replaced the prompt with a one-token placeholder. Prefill ran a trivial forward pass on that one token.
  4. KV transfer. Prefill sent one page of KV to decode and signaled that the transfer was complete.
  5. Decode admission. Decode's admission queue had the same finished() check, so it accepted the handoff.
  6. Decode attention. Decode started generating and attention read all 8 reserved pages. Only page P0 had been written by this request. Pages P1 to P7 still held what earlier requests left in them: other users' prompts and partial generations.
  7. Response. The client got HTTP 200 instead of HTTP 400. prompt_tokens matched the long prompt and the reply was coherent. It arrived faster than an 8-page prefill should take, and it contained content from other users' KV pages.

Every request over the threshold behaved this way. This bug had been reported to SGLang by another user as issue #30233 on July 6, 2026, which Cloudflare noticed while investigating this incident. We had been flagging these types of issues with SGLang since v0.5.10 and this security incident sped up work that Cloudflare had already started in collaboration with the SGLang team. The patch for this issue was released in SGLang v0.5.20, with follow-ups in v0.5.21 and v0.5.22, and is available for all other operators dependent on SGLang to use. We highly recommend all operators update SGLang dependencies to v0.5.22 or later. For more details on specific PRs, read on below.

GLM 5.3 was the only model affected by this bug. Every other disaggregated deployment on Workers AI has KV pools larger than its context length on both prefill and decode, so no request could reach the rejection path. We have applied the engine fix and the hardening described below to every model we serve with SGLang, and our deployment checks require them for every new deployment.

Timeline

All times UTC.

When

What

GLM 5.3 launched on Workers AI with a prefill KV pool smaller than its context window. The exposure was present from launch.

Sep 8, 2026 - 23:11

Report received via HackerOne.

Sep 9, 2026 - 08:00

Cloudflare begins verifying the HackerOne report.

Sep 9, 2026 - 13:22

Security incident declared. Product Security reproduced the leak using two independent accounts within 25 minutes.

Sep 9, 2026 - 14:00

After confirming the scope of the issue, GLM 5.3 was set to private. Requests return HTTP 400. Status page updated.

Sep 9, 2026 - 14:35

Root cause identified as the prefill pool being smaller than the context length. Canary prefill node with a larger pool confirmed not susceptible.

Sep 9, 2026 - 14:52

All prefill nodes rolled to the corrected configuration.

Sep 9, 2026 - 19:04

Full deployment rebuilt with the corrected configuration plus a Cloudflare-authored engine patch that correctly returns errors for requests rejected by the prefill scheduler. Validated against the researcher's reproduction script.

Sep 9, 2026 - 19:40

Model restored to public.

Sep 10, 2026 - 23:30

Ongoing hardening effort

This bug belongs to a class of KV cache memory-safety bugs that Cloudflare has been working to address for several months. In each case, a page is freed, reused, or read while something else still has a claim on it. We see two common causes.

The first is page lifetime within a single node. Several tasks on a decode node can hold the same page at once: token generation, offload to host memory, the KV transfer receiver, and the abort and error paths. If one of them frees the page while another is still using it, a new request can be given that page while it is still being read or written. Our earlier fixes for decode offload (#24226, #30899) and double release on grammar errors (#30937) were of this kind.

The second is a race across nodes. When a request is aborted while prefill is still writing its KV cache to decode over RDMA, the writes already sent cannot be recalled. If decode frees those pages right away, those pages can be given to another request, and the late writes land in that request's KV cache. Cloudflare has contributed to the effort to fix this race through proposed fixes (#31357, #38961) and a reproduction script (#32564). In both cases the result is corrupted output, or one user's data in another user's response, with no error raised. The bug in this incident was different: a rejected request went through the handoff every time, rather than by a timing accident. But it had the same result: decode reading pages this request never wrote. None of these covered the failure in this incident in which prefill rejected the request, and decode never learned of it.

Since the incident, we have:

  • Extended deferred release to hold prefill's source pages as well, and to cover every failure type, not just aborts. We proposed it upstream as #38961, which was superseded by #40645, #41402, and #41404.
  • Deployed bounded Mooncake transfer batches (#32758, from the SGLang community), so no single transfer call can outlast the release timeout.
  • Changed our load balancer so a client disconnect no longer aborts a request mid-transfer. It holds the prefill connection until prefill finishes and the decode connection until the first token, then closes both.
  • Added a check to every disaggregated deployment change: KV pool size measured against context length, deferred release on both roles, transfer batch bounds inside the release timeout, and all required patches applied.

All of these changes were released to our disaggregated production deployments.

Working with the SGLang team

We met with the SGLang maintainers at RadixArk on September 10, the day after the incident. We agreed that RadixArk would investigate the race conditions we had reported, upstream the integrity-checking idea, and build reproduction tests for this class of bug.

The following have landed on SGLang main to address this incident and related KV cache race conditions, and all but one are included in v0.5.22. Operators running disaggregated SGLang should update to v0.5.22 or backport these patches as needed.

What we recommend to other operators

If you run SGLang in disaggregated prefill/decode mode, we recommend the following:

  1. Measure your KV pool and compare it to your context length, on every prefill and decode node, from the engine's startup log, after every change to weights, quantization, parallelism, or memory fraction. If the pool is smaller, lower the context length to fit. Do not rely on a proxy to enforce the limit, and do not assume the engine will reject what does not fit. This is the check we did not enforce.
  2. Upgrade to a build that includes #36988 and #38935 (v0.5.22 or later), so an over-length request is rejected before handoff regardless of pool size. This is the engine-side fix, and it is the backstop for the day your check in step one is wrong.
  3. Run with deferred KV release on both roles (default after #41023), and bound your Mooncake transfer batches so a single timed-out call cannot leave an unbounded tail of writes.
  4. Turn on corruption detection where your model supports it. --disaggregation-enable-kv-checksum and --kv-canary do not yet cover every model architecture. Check your logs to confirm requests are being verified. We are working with the SGLang team to extend both checks to more architectures, including GLM 5.3, GLM 5.3 Flash, and DeepSeek V4.
  5. Ensure your proxy is not generating unnecessary aborts. Configure your load balancer to allow requests to proceed up to the first token, so that you do not trigger an abort that requires cross-node coordination.

Longer term

Integrity by construction

Configuration checks and lifecycle fixes reduce the number of ways a page can be misused. They do not make misuse impossible, and this incident is a reminder that the next bug will have a shape we have not seen. The durable answer is for the engine to detect, at read time, that a request is about to attend over a page it does not own, and fail that one request rather than return someone else's data.

We built a prototype of this over the summer and described it in August. Every physical KV page carries a tag that changes when the page is reallocated, each request records the tags it expects, and the mapping is checked before decode reads the cache. In our tests it cost under 1% in throughput and tail latency. We tested it on GLM 5.2 in mid-August, but disabled it shortly afterwards due to reliability issues.

The prototype was also tied to specific attention backends and model architectures, so it could not be a general fix. We are working with the SGLang team to build a production version into the engine that works across every model, rather than maintaining Cloudflare-specific patches. The per-transfer checksum in #39500 is a first step: it validates the handoff from prefill to decode. Page-level tags go further, because they check every read, including reads long after the transfer.

Integrity by mathematical impossibility

RDMA copies data directly from one node’s memory to another’s. It’s vital for the two machines to agree on where the data goes, how large it is, and when it’s finished; any mismatch can cause the receiver to read the wrong data. This bug is an example of a consistency failure in a distributed system, in which the two machines had inconsistent views of the state of that system.

Elsewhere in Cloudflare, we have put effort into proving the safety of distributed systems using formal verification methods. Topaz enables conflict-free IP selection for our authoritative DNS servers. Models of Meerkat’s QuePaxa implementation have demonstrated consistency bugs that were subsequently fixed.

We are now directing our experience in formal methods to KV cache transfer engines. This will start with modeling and proving the safety of an RDMA-based KV cache transfer protocol. The goal is to model our production SGLang’s distributed KV cache system using Mooncake, then track and fix any divergence from the safety properties we want to guarantee. The aim is to prove — as far as possible — that a bug like this cannot occur again. Realistically, we expect gaps in what the provers can tell us, but proving the rest of the system allows us to more closely review and monitor those gaps.

Coordinated disclosure

We are publishing this report as part of a coordinated disclosure. We want to thank the researcher, Gadi Evron, who reported this through our HackerOne program with a clear, reproducible script and gave us time to fix it and to coordinate with the SGLang maintainers before publishing. We also want to thank the SGLang team at RadixArk, who treated this as their problem as well as ours and landed the upstream fixes with urgency.

Read more at the post from the SGLang team.

If you find a security issue in Workers AI, please report it at hackerone.com/cloudflare.

item.title: Introducing Clairic, a new System One class of extraction models
item.description: Clairic is a new model from Cloudflare that is a System One extraction modeI, capable of extracting, computing, estimating, and forecasting data from unstructured inputs.
item.dc:creator: Alex Reneau
Michelle Chen
Kevin Flansburg
item.content:encoded:
Today, we're announcing a preview of a new class of System One-style models: extraction models. Our first one, Clairic, is available hosted on Workers AI as @cf/cloudflare/clairic.We intend to release the model open-weights soon. Clairic is an extraction model that is able to extract, compute, estimate, and forecast values from unstructured inputs — all at a significantly higher accuracy, faster latency, and cheaper cost than traditional LLMs.

Context

When System One models were announced by TypeSafe a month ago, it took the industry by storm. As referenced by TypeSafe in their blog and defined by Daniel Kahneman’s book Thinking, Fast and Slow, a System One model should be fast and precise, which contrasts a System Two model that is capable of deliberate reasoning (like LLMs). With this, TypeSafe introduced Jev — a model that is purpose-fit for a specific use case, and priced accessibly given its niche domain. It excelled where LLMs failed, helping users make decisions based on probabilities and well-typed outputs. The introduction of Jev prompted people to start thinking about a new class of models that were not LLMs and how to integrate them into their workflows.

We were inspired by the concept of System One models and started thinking about other tasks where LLMs are inefficient. There are many structured-output calls going to frontier LLMs today with the same shapes again and again: What's the invoice total? When was this delivered? How many days late is it? What will this repair cost? What will traffic look like over the next 24 hours? None of these have answers you can list out in advance, which is needed for a decision model to give probabilities against. That led us to the class of models we're introducing today: System One extraction models.

Introducing System One extraction models

Until now, every System One model has been a decision model: Jev and Clef take an input state and a list of questions and give probabilities against the inputs and your listed questions. Clairic is the first model in a new class: System One extraction models. It is still fast, typed, and cheap, but it answers with values directly extracted from the input, computed from it, or predicted beyond it.

Most model tasks ask for one of three kinds of output: a number, a choice from a fixed set, or open-ended text. Clairic handles the first, returning numbers with an 80% range, and also pulls typed values like names, dates and lists out of the input. Clef handles the second: it picks among options and returns a probability for each. LLMs handle the third. We call Clairic and Clef System One models because they answer in a single pass, without reasoning or generating tokens. They charge only for input and typically respond in under a second, while an LLM that reasons through the same step takes several seconds.

An extraction model can return:

  • Extracted values: Text copied from the input, such as a name, an order ID or a description. Each one comes back as a span with its character offsets and a confidence score.
  • Including, computed values: Numbers, dates, times, datetimes, durations and lists, read from the input or worked out from it. They follow the rules of their type (for example, two decimals for cents) and come with a confidence score.
  • Estimated values: Values the input doesn't state but gives evidence for. Each one comes back as a distribution inside the bounds you declare, on the grid you specify, with a median and an 80% interval.
  • Forecasted values: Future values of a series, one estimate per step ahead, each with its own 80% interval.

And because it generates no tokens, it can't produce a mistyped answer or “hallucinate” in the same way as an LLM (though it can, of course, make mistakes). Outputs are a value of the type you asked for, or null when the model fails to find an answer in the input. It also comes with confidence scores against the outputs to help you evaluate if it is appropriate to trust the model or to take a second look.

Here’s how extraction models fit into the landscape of System One and System Two models:

Together, these models can work together in unison to help you get closer to parsing through real-world data, making decisions on inputs, and then taking actions. Extraction models turn raw input into typed values, decision models turn values into decisions, and LLMs turn decisions into words.

How a request works

Clairic is designed differently than an LLM. Similar to a decision model, it only processes input tokens with a single forward pass, and thus has no charge for output tokens. It is much faster, cheaper, and more accurate than an LLM for certain use cases.

A request is a state (the text to read, plus up to four optional images) and a map of typed fields. You name each field, give it a type and optional plain-language instructions, and get back one typed answer per field, all from one parallel pass. There is no reasoning and no output tokens – everything computes in a single forward pass, which means it is both fast and cheap.

Type

Returns

text

A specific span of the input, with its offsets

number

A number read or computed, honoring integer and decimals

date, time, datetime

Calendar dates and valid times, in ISO form

duration

A length of time in the unit you choose

list

Matching text, number or date, in input order

estimate

A distribution inside your [min, max], on your step grid, linear or log scale.

forecast

One estimate per future step of a series

Every scalar answer comes with p_null (the probability that the value isn’t in the inputs) and confidence. Every estimate answer comes with a median and an 80% interval (p10 to p90), plus all 99 percentiles on request. There's no limit on the number of fields: if they don't fit beside the input in one pass, the server splits them into parallel passes that each see the whole input, then merges the answers.

Here are some examples to illustrate the model’s features. Of course, using these features in a workflow would require appropriate inputs.

An example: Extracting values

Extraction is probably the most common job handed to LLMs today: "return the invoice number, vendor and due date as JSON." It works most of the time, but the failure modes are hard to catch. The output may not be valid JSON, a digit can be misread as it's generated, and once a text excerpt comes back, there's no way to trace it to where it appeared in the source. Most people build extraction pipelines to combat this, with multiple layers of parsing, schema validation, retries and spot checks. On top of that, you pay for reasoning and output tokens on every field of every document.

Clairic operates differently; it doesn’t generate text answers. Instead, you get:

  • Values extracted from your input, so an answer is grounded.
  • Computed values, so it can parse through unstructured data without pre-sanitizing it.
  • Character offset spans, so you can reference where in the input the data was.
  • Confidence labels, so you can determine which values need a second look.
  • A strongly typed output, so numbers and dates are formed under the rules of their type (e.g., a cents field has two decimals).
  • Handling for null values, where a missing field returns with null as an answer (along with an estimated probability of null and a guess).
  • Cheaper and faster answers, because every field is answered in the same parallel pass. So asking for thirty fields costs about the same as asking for three.

Let’s walk through an example to illustrate the ways Clairic can extract values from unstructured data and make estimates. Take a customer support email:

Hi, order A-88412 arrived on Sept 28, 2026 with a cracked screen and a dented corner. I paid $649.00 plus $52.10 tax. It's now Oct 9, 2026 and I'd like this fixed or refunded. Thanks, Dana

From a Worker, you would make a request to Clairic to process this data:

const { answers } = await env.AI.run("@cf/cloudflare/clairic", {
  state: email,
  fields: {
    order_id:            { type: "text", instructions: "Order number" },
    delivered_on:        { type: "date", instructions: "Delivery date" },
    amount_paid:         { type: "number", decimals: 2, unit: "USD", instructions: "Total paid including tax" },
    days_since_delivery: { type: "duration", unit: "days", integer: true,
                           instructions: "Days from delivery to the date the customer wrote" },
    damage:              { type: "list", items: "text", instructions: "Each kind of damage described" },
    tracking_number:     { type: "text" },
  },
});

Clairic returns the extracted values, spans in the input, probability that it is null (p_null) and confidence score:

{
  "order_id": {
    "type": "text",
    "p_null": 3.4e-6,
    "span": [10, 17],
    "guess": "A-88412",
    "confidence": 0.999957,
    "value": "A-88412"
  },
  "delivered_on": {
    "type": "date",
    "p_null": 6.5e-8,
    "guess": "2026-09-28",
    "confidence": 0.999999,
    "value": "2026-09-28"
  },
  "amount_paid": {
    "type": "number",
    "p_null": 1.6e-5,
    "guess": 701.1,
    "confidence": 0.999944,
    "value": 701.1
  },
  "days_since_delivery": {
    "type": "duration",
    "p_null": 6.1e-9,
    "unit": "days",
    "guess": 11,
    "confidence": 0.999999,
    "value": 11
  },
  "damage": {
    "type": "list",
    "value": ["cracked screen", "dented corner"],
    "spans": [[50, 64], [71, 84]]
  },
  "tracking_number": {
    "type": "text",
    "p_null": 1,
    "span": [106, 112],
    "guess": "$52.10",
    "confidence": 0.416016,
    "value": null
  }
}

A few things to notice:

  • amount_paid isn't written anywhere in the email. In this example, Clairic added the price and the tax in the same pass and returns the sum.
  • days_since_delivery is also worked out from two dates in the text, not directly in the input.
  • damage lists both kinds of damage as exact spans, so you can highlight them in the source.
  • tracking_number isn't in the email, so it comes back null instead of a plausible-looking guess. guess shows what the model would otherwise have picked.

Clairic also works with images

Here’s a real-life photo of a receipt — the text is not perfect and the angle of the image doesn’t help its legibility. We passed this image to Clairic to see what it could extract:

  "model": "clairic",
  "answers": {
   "order_number": {
    "type": "number",
    "p_null": 0.0040206750854849815,
    "guess": 77245,
    "confidence": 0.776249383996532,
    "value": 77245
   },
   "purchased_at": {
    "type": "datetime",
    "p_null": 4.136094133855295e-08,
    "guess": "2026-07-01T13:34:00",
    "confidence": 0.831464227002992,
    "value": "2026-07-01T13:34:00"
   },
   "quantity": {
    "type": "number",
    "p_null": 5.2313655629632194e-08,
    "guess": 2,
    "confidence": 0.9997007500403496,
    "value": 2
   },
   "unit_price": {
    "type": "number",
    "p_null": 0.001599092734977603,
    "guess": 7.99,
    "confidence": 0.9991279019989127,
    "value": 7.99
   },

    "type": "number",
    "p_null": 9.69956488461321e-08,
    "guess": 15.98,
    "confidence": 0.9999881983893096,
    "value": 15.98
   },
   "sales_tax": {
    "type": "number",
    "p_null": 2.5511653802823275e-06,
    "guess": 0,
    "confidence": 0.9999800924450729,
    "value": 0
   },

    "type": "number",
    "p_null": 5.953857908025384e-05,
    "guess": 2.39,

   },

    "type": "number",
    "p_null": 0.9994148015975952,

    "confidence": 0.91852733929319,
    "value": null
   }

}

As you can see, it was able to extract all the values from the images, alongside a confidence score. It also correctly stated that there was no discount shown in the receipt, giving the value as null.

An example: Estimating values

Some values aren't in the input at all, but the input carries evidence for them. For example, values might not be in plain text but can be discerned from values around it. If you ask an LLM for an estimation, you usually get a single number with no sense of how sure the model is. It will make safe guesses or hallucinate, or reason its way around the answer. If you land on an estimate, any downstream processing can't tell a confident $180 from an unconfident $180, so it can't help you decide what is appropriate to automate in the circumstances. It is also a lot slower and more expensive to do reasoning through LLMs.

A decision model can approximate an estimate by choosing among buckets ("under $100", "$100–500", …), but buckets are coarse, every bucket adds input tokens, and each new category adds more sources of confusion for the model during its decision making process.

Clairic returns a distribution over the range you declare: a point value, a median, an 80% interval, and every percentile on request. The estimate is designed to fall inside your bounds, so there's nothing to clamp or round afterward. The width of the interval reflects data confidence: a narrow range signals high certainty, while a wide range indicates low certainty, information you can use to route another check.

Here’s another example, where Clairic looks at historical home prices and comparable sales, to determine an estimate :

const { answers } = await env.AI.run("@cf/cloudflare/clairic", {
  state: `Comparable sales:
sqft,beds,year_built,neighborhood,sale_price
1450,3,1998,Elm Park,412000
2100,4,2006,Elm Park,585000
980,2,1975,Riverside,265000
1600,3,2003,Elm Park,449000
1300,3,1990,Riverside,318000

Subject property:
sqft,beds,year_built,neighborhood
1620,3,2001,Elm Park`,
  fields: {
    sale_price:     { type: "estimate", unit: "USD", min: 50000, max: 5000000, scale: "log", step: 1000 }
});

Clairic will return an estimated value:

{
  "sale_price":     { "type": "estimate", "value": 418000, "median": 415000, "p10": 370000, "p90": 470000, "p_below": 0.0, "p_above": 0.0 }
}

Values always fall inside your bounds, and the width of the interval shows how much the input informs the prediction: price is narrow ($370,000-$470,000), days on market is wide (24-148). Because fields are unlimited and answered in parallel, you can score many items in one call (one estimate per candidate, lead, or listing) and sort them in code.

An example: Forecasting values

Forecasting values in a time series is quite hard for generalized models — it usually means you have to either build a specific pipeline per metric (parse the data, fit a model, tune it, deploy it), or you paste 36 months of numbers into an LLM and ask for the next three. The first is accurate but really expensive and time-consuming to set up for every new series. The second is easy, but you get point forecasts with no intervals, forecasts that shift depending on how the prompt is worded, and answers with limited confidence.

Clairic sits between the two — it is not claiming to replace a dedicated time-series model, but it is a little faster and cheaper than your regular LLM. A forecast field takes the history as plain text in state and returns, for every step ahead, a value and an 80% interval, inside the bounds you declare. It reads the history the way you already have it, whether that's a CSV export, a pasted dashboard, or rows mixed with notes, and may often work with no need to clean up your data beforehand.

To see how that holds up on real data, we used a public series: the number of people the Transportation Security Administration (TSA) screens at U.S. airport checkpoints each day. Each morning we asked Clairic for the next day's count, given the real counts so far, for 21 days in a row:

const { answers } = await env.AI.run("@cf/cloudflare/clairic", {
  state: `Daily number of people screened at TSA checkpoints at US airports.
date,weekday,travelers
2026-07-16,Thu,2850229
...
2026-10-13,Tue,2353356
Forecast date: 2026-10-14 (Wed)`,
  fields: {
    travelers: { type: "forecast", horizon: 1, interval: "day",
                 min: 500000, max: 4000000, scale: "log",
                 instructions: "Number of people screened tomorrow" },
  },
});

Which returns:

{
  "travelers": { "type": "forecast", "value": [2416117], "median": [2419283], "p10": [2270774], "p90": [2556769] }
}

In actuality, TSA screened 2,419,474 people that day, which is right around the median 2,419,283 that Clairic predicted.

Data: TSA checkpoint travel numbers, accessed Oct. 15, 2026.

Across the 21 days, Clairic's forecasts were off by 3.3% on average, and 17 of the 21 actual counts landed inside its 80% interval, which follows what an 80% interval should do. It picked up the weekly rhythm from the numbers alone: quieter Tuesdays and Saturdays, busier Thursdays, Fridays, and Sundays.

The misses are also interesting: three of the four days outside the interval fall on the Columbus Day weekend, when more people flew than the previous weeks suggested. Clairic forecasts from the patterns in the series but doesn't account for events the series doesn't show, like holidays.

Thinking fast and slow

These models are designed to fit alongside your existing agentic workflows. An extraction model predicts values, a decision model decides what to do with these values, and an LLM takes action with them. It is a perfect marriage between System One and System Two models. It bridges the existing gap, where you either have to manually extract data for LLMs, or have an LLM parse through messy data (which is costly, time-consuming, and can lead to hallucinations). With System One extraction models, you can work with real-world data with more speed, efficiency, and precision.

Here's an example of the damaged-product claim from earlier, illustrating how all the models can work together.  We built this into a live demo you can try here.

// 1. Clairic turns the email into values
const facts = (await env.AI.run("@cf/cloudflare/clairic", {
  state: email,
  fields: {
    customer_name:       { type: "text", instructions: "Customer's first name" },
    order_id:            { type: "text", instructions: "Order number" },
    amount_paid:         { type: "number", decimals: 2, unit: "USD", instructions: "Total paid including tax" },
    days_since_delivery: { type: "duration", unit: "days", integer: true,
                           instructions: "Days from delivery to the date the customer wrote" },
    damage:              { type: "list", items: "text", instructions: "Each kind of damage described" },
    repair_cost:         { type: "estimate", unit: "USD", min: 10, max: 5000, scale: "log", step: 1,
                           instructions: "Cost to repair the damage described" },
  },
})).answers;
const { customer_name, order_id, amount_paid, days_since_delivery, damage, repair_cost } = facts;

// 2. Clef decides from Clairic's values and the policy, not from the raw email
const options = {
  refund:  "Full refund of the amount paid",
  repair:  "Free repair, with a prepaid shipping label",
};
const { choice } = (await env.AI.run("@cf/cloudflare/clef", {
  state: `Damage claim for order ${order_id.value}.
Paid: $${amount_paid.value.toFixed(2)}. Delivered ${days_since_delivery.value} days ago.
Damage reported: ${damage.value.join(", ")}.
Estimated repair cost: $${repair_cost.median} (80% range $${repair_cost.p10}-$${repair_cost.p90}).
Policy: refunds within 30 days of delivery. Prefer repair when it costs less than 60% of the price and the damage doesn't stop the product from working.`,
  questions: {
    resolution: { type: "choice", instructions: "What should we offer?", criteria: options },
  },
})).answers.resolution;

// 3. An LLM writes the reply, from the decision and the facts it needs
const { response } = await env.AI.run("@cf/zai-org/glm-5.3", {
  messages: [{
    role: "user",
    content: `Write a short, warm reply to ${customer_name.value}. Use only these facts: order ${order_id.value}; ` +
             `damage: ${damage.value.join(", ")}; what happens next: ${options[choice]}. Under 60 words.`,
  }],
});

Each step gets cleaner input than the one before. Clef decides from a five-line summary of typed values instead of a free-form email, which can also be susceptible to prompt injection. The LLM never sees the email, only the decision and the predictions it needs, so there are fewer numbers for it to misuse. Every step is typed and auditable, and only one step generates text. In the all-LLM version of this pipeline, all three steps are generative calls, and every value in the reply has to be checked by hand.

We ran this pipeline against an all-LLM version with GLM-5.3 writing the reply in both. In the all-LLM version, GLM-5.3 also does the extraction and the decision, from the same email, policy and prompts:

Clairic → Clef → GLM-5.3

The cascade finished in 19.3 seconds against 61.7 seconds: 69% less time, or about 3.2 times faster. Clairic and Clef handled extraction and the decision in under a second combined, where GLM-5.3 took 38 seconds for the same two steps. It also costs 49% less to use the cascaded pipeline vs the all-LLM pipeline. With GLM, both pipelines got the facts and the decision right in every run, but Clairic's repair estimate was identical each time, while GLM-5.3's changed on every run ($250, $250 and $220, with different ranges each time).

Notably, under the all-LLM pipeline both Gemma 4 and Qwen failed at this task, as they were unable to deduce values like repair_cost from the inputs, showing how LLMs are not great at data extraction tasks.

Preview release

Today, we're releasing a hosted endpoint for Clairic on Workers AI. We intend to release the model with open weights soon. We wanted to take the time first to introduce the concept of a System One extraction model, so you can start thinking about how this class of model would fit into appropriate workflows.

The current endpoint is an early checkpoint and we expect it to get better. Here are our early impressions:

  • Reading is strong, but multi-step arithmetic isn't yet. One- and two-step calculations (totals, differences, conversions, date arithmetic) seem reliable. Longer chains of dependent steps are hard for any one-pass model without a scratchpad. The same goes for aggregating across many rows of a table. At least for now, have Clairic predict the value and let code do the math.
  • Estimates need evidence. Clairic estimates best from comparables, history, or descriptive text in the input. Asking it for a value it has no evidence for may be limited in specificity.
  • Calibration is measured, not guaranteed. Intervals are trained to be calibrated and are on most held-out sets, but they can run narrow on unfamiliar data.
  • Forecasting is basic. The model is not designed to accurately replace or predict time-series models that are trained on specific data. You should use it where appropriate, such as non-critical, general pattern matching, not detailed long-horizon forecasting.
  • Use confidence. The architecture makes every answer well formed, not necessarily correct. Use confidence, p_null and the intervals to decide what to automate (in an appropriate workflow context) and what to send off for additional review.

We'll keep working on the arithmetic, estimation and forecasting sides of the model with each checkpoint. After some more work, we plan to release the model open-weights for everyone to play around with as well.

Try it out

Clairic is available as a preview on Workers AI as @cf/cloudflare/clairic. Call it from a Worker with env.AI.run(), or from anywhere with the REST API. We have full model docs here, as well as a new docs explainer on how the extraction model API looks.

P.S. Since you liked the etymology of the name Clef, here’s how we landed on the name Clairic. We started with a desire to keep the name of the model thematically and sonically similar to Clef. Clair came to mind, sharing the same “cl” sound, as well as roots in music (“Clair de Lune”). More importantly, we wanted the name to be descriptive to the nature of the model. The Clairic model should be able to help you with clerical tasks like extracting data clearly from a corpus of inputs and upholding accuracy in tasks like bookkeeping. The prediction aspect of the model leans into the “Clair” root — allowing you to estimate and predict future values, similar to clairvoyance. Lastly, we like the idea of having this be [Cl]oudflare’s [AI R]egression model. Thus, Clairic was born into the world. We hope you enjoy it.

item.title: Introducing Clef-omni with full multimodality, plus a faster Clef and a cheaper Clef-flash
item.description: We are expanding the Clef decision model family with Clef-omni, natively processing audio, video, images, and text in a single pipeline. We’ve also lowered Clef-flash pricing and boosted Clef inference speeds by up to 2.0x.
item.dc:creator: Michelle Chen
Alex Reneau
Kevin Jain
item.content:encoded:
Following last week’s release of Clef and Clef-flash, Cloudflare’s open-weight decision models, we decided to bring forth more gifts. Today, we’re releasing Clef-omni, which takes in audio and video input alongside text and image. We also cut the price of Clef-flash so it is now cheaper than Jev, and we made Clef faster.

Although the model game is still early for Cloudflare, innovation and iteration is in our DNA, and we apply these principles to everything we do. In fact, the story of Clef came together over the course of less than a week. We decided we wanted to do something in the decision model space on a Friday evening, trained the model over the weekend, and launched it on Thursday. Even with such a short timeline, we were able to ship performant, high-quality, open-weight models for the community — imagine what more we can do in the future.

For today, we’re excited to keep up the momentum with new additions and improvements to our Clef family of models. This is just the beginning, and we’ll continue to get better, faster, cheaper, and more innovative.

Clef-omni takes audio, video, image, and text input

Our new Clef-omni model is able to take audio, video, image, and text input. This changes the paradigm for decision models, which have been largely text-only since the debut of Jev from TypeSafe. With Clef, we supported images and video frame arrays, but Clef-omni is able to take in audio (wav or mp3) and video (mp4 or webm) alongside text and images.

Instead of setting up cascading pipelines of models that transcribe speech-to-text, or splitting audio and image channels from video, you can just call one model to make decisions across any modality. We are now one step closer to a model that is able to interact with the world as we experience it — through audio, visual, and textual communication, all in one.

Check out our developer docs for the new Clef-omni model. We also released the model open-weights on HuggingFace. For a quick start, here’s how you can send new modality inputs to Clef-omni:

curl https://api.cloudflare.com/client/v4/accounts/$CLOUDFLARE_ACCOUNT_ID/ai/run/@cf/cloudflare/clef-omni \
  -X POST \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer $CLOUDFLARE_AUTH_TOKEN" \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d '{
    "model": "clef-omni",
    "state": "Review the installation: a photo of the unit, an audio recording of it running, and a video of the fan.",
    "images": ["data:image/png;base64,<base64-png>"],
    "audio": ["data:audio/mpeg;base64,<base64-mp3>"],
    "videos": ["data:video/mp4;base64,<base64-mp4>"],
    "questions": {
      "label_visible": {"type": "noul", "instructions": "Is the model and serial number label visible in the photo?"},
      "sounds_normal": {"type": "noul", "instructions": "Does the unit sound like it is running smoothly, without rattling or grinding?"},
      "fan_running": {"type": "noul", "instructions": "Is the fan running in the video?"}
    }
  }'

Clef-omni expands our open-weight decision architecture to natively handle multimodal workflows. We built this on a Qwen3-Omni-30B-A3B-Instruct mixture-of-experts (MoE) foundation, where the model was already capable of processing text, imagery, audio, and video directly within a single pipeline. However, we adopt the primary comprehension backbone while discarding the text-to-speech output components. In production, Clef-omni executes a quick prefill pass across the complete payload, scoring all modalities and valid parameter options simultaneously.

Because we skip output token generation since Clef models are not Large Language Models (LLMs), we remove the overhead of transcribing or captioning incoming files. Media elements map straight into the unified sequence, where video and audio are synced with visual frames for joint processing. Clef-omni then pulls candidate values directly from internal embeddings using our two-stage attention routing: every valid option gathers key evidence from the input (regardless if they are buried in text snippets, visual elements, or audio streams) before field vectors cross-attend across the full context to compute confidence scores. We add a built-in lexical grammar that preserves option semantics, so that we can deliver fast, schema-constrained scoring across every input type.

We train the model with the same techniques as we did with Clef — freezing the Qwen3 backbone, training low-rank adapters (LoRA), and applying our standard post-training approach: combining label-smoothed cross-entropy loss with Brier score calibration. The result is a model that is resilient and designed to succeed regardless of schema variations, field ordering, and prompt structures.

This brings several core upgrades to the Clef model family. Calibrated, schema-bound decisions now seamlessly handle text, images, audio, and synchronized video in a single API call. It's also fast. Text-only decisions return in about 130 ms at the median, image inputs in about 150 ms, and audio clips in a few hundred milliseconds. Even a full 21-second video clip with sound is scored in about 1.5 seconds, all in a single API call.

How are people using Clef?

At Cloudflare, we’ve had teams experimenting with Clef as a model that can help classify over general domains. The coolest thing about watching teams adopt Clef is that the capability to do detections and classifications have moved into the model layer, where it is accessible for anyone to start incorporating decision models into their use cases. Previously, even with zero-shot classifiers, the small models may not have been powerful enough to classify across any domain without further tuning. You might have needed to stand up a specialized machine learning team to help train over your particular domain, and gather a corpus of data in order to train a better model. Now, all you need to do is call a model to instantly parse through input data with precision.

A few highlights of how teams at Cloudflare are using Clef: Our public GitHub docs repo uses Clef to instantly detect and close spam issues. EmDash, our content management system, moderates plugin libraries for phishing. Thank you for all the love and warm reception around Cloudflare’s first models — we are focused on bringing you more. Try out our Clef family of models, and tell us what you think.

item.title: Introducing Clef: Our open-source decision models, and new RL fine-tuning platform
item.description: We are introducing Clef and Clef-flash, open-source decision models hosted on Workers AI for high-speed classification and agentic workflows. Also launching: a new reinforcement learning platform that allows developers to fine-tune decision models using their own data.
item.dc:creator: Michelle Chen
Alex Reneau
Kevin Flansburg
item.content:encoded:
Over the last few weeks, there has been lots of buzz around decision models such as Typesafe AI’s Jev System One model. While classifier models have been around for some time, Jev introduces a new decision model concept into the world of AI — a model that produces bounded structured outputs cheaply, quickly and consistently that can be added into a workflow when a decision is required. These models are capable enough to work over any set of inputs without constantly retraining the model to incorporate new classification categories. This contrasts with the world of Large Language Models (LLMs), which are largely non-deterministic, but are open-ended enough to reason and generate text and tool calls for agentic workloads. 

Today, we’re releasing two Cloudflare-trained decision models, Clef and Clef-flash, hosted on Workers AI. Clef is currently the leader when evaluated against the Jev Decision Index, you can view full results on the live benchmark demo site. These models are smarter, faster, and fully Jev-API compatible, so you can experiment with these hosted models easily. We’re fully open-sourcing these models on Hugging Face under an Apache 2.0 license for you to run locally and experiment with yourselves. 

Lastly, we’re excited to debut our new reinforcement learning (RL) product, which allows customers to fine-tune Clef to suit their use cases as well.

What is a decision model?

A decision model makes classifications to help agents decide how to act, based on certain probabilities. For example, you can pass in a customer support message (inputs) and ask if it is urgent and which team should handle it. A decision model will return typed answers with probabilities (outputs), which your code can use to route the ticket, trigger an escalation, or defer to a human. This means that a human does not necessarily need to be in the loop for agentic decisions anymore — agents can programmatically gather context, make decisions, and take actions on tasks, or defer to a human when needed.

Specifically at Cloudflare, we’ve been testing our new Clef model on our Threat Intelligence team to help us classify website domains. By giving a domain to Clef (with Browser Run) it can quickly identify categories that the domain falls under — for example, it might classify a domain with a 95% chance it is a fashion website, 85% ecommerce, <1% phishing, etc. This classification took our Clef model 2.2s to fetch, render, and classify the website. In contrast, our fastest general LLM gpt-oss-120b took 4.7s in the same workflow, and only returned two classifications. As a user, you can imagine how a 2x savings in latency and results can help us improve our threat intelligence workflows and be faster in identifying malicious or legitimate domains. Generalize this to any use case where you need to make quick programmatic decisions, and you unlock powerful agentic workflows that are able to autonomously decide, reason, and execute.

In music theory, a clef is a symbol placed at the beginning of a musical staff that assigns specific pitch names to the lines and spaces. A decision model is analogous to a music clef because it helps define the domain of the context and the subsequent notes (actions) that follow it. We chose Clef as the name of our family of decision models, as it serves similar purposes, and the CF hearkens to Cloudflare.

How is Clef different from other decision models?

Although the market is getting increasingly saturated with decision models, Clef has some unique properties that make us excited to release it to the public. First, it has a vision encoder so it’s able to take in images and classify visual content. This is different from Jev, which only does text classification today. Secondly, our model has a 64k context window (compared to Jev’s 32k), which allows users to squeeze more input state for the model to classify against.

Third, our model is accurate and powerful, scoring competitively against other decision models on the market across various quality benchmarks. Clef also produces strictly typed outputs similar to Jev and is fully API-compatible, so you can make the swap extremely easily. The larger Clef model is your more powerful precision model, while the Clef-Flash model is great for latency-critical decisions. The models are enterprise-ready with our guarantee that we don’t read, store, or train on your requests or responses (unless you want to use our fine-tuning product, which we go into below). You can get started with the Clef models today, starting with our developer documentation or play around with the open-source model on the Hugging Face repo.

If you’d like help tuning Clef for a specific workload, we are also offering fine-tuning services — first as a hands-on partner with our forward-deployed engineer (FDE) team, and then later as a self-serve fine-tuning platform for customers to train and redeploy the model onto Cloudflare.

How we trained Clef

In the same week that Jev came out, we posted about some experiments we had with our own homegrown decision model. Our demo goes into how we adapted the DiffusionGemma model to output deterministic probabilities by exposing the logprobs that are generated by a large language model. Our initial approach built upon independent research by Matt Mastracci, who has been active in the machine learning (ML) community with sharing new ideas and pull requests to vLLM inference engine to make DiffusionGemma support stronger.

Clef builds upon this concept, but uses a different base model as the backbone. We currently use Qwen as the base model and post-trained it to suit decision model use cases. During inference, Clef uses Qwen for a prefill-only pass, then scores the valid schema choices in parallel. The decision step is non-autoregressive, so there’s no intermediate text to generate token by token, making Clef significantly faster than autoregressive LLMs. Rather than generating intermediate text to produce structured answers, Clef and Clef-flash derive schema choices directly from internal backbone representations. This approach relies on a specialized two-stage attention routing process: every valid choice extracts context relevant to the prompt, allowing individual field parameters to cross-attend with other fields and back to the original payload prior to scoring. By leveraging a lexical prior, the model preserves semantic intent across options. Ultimately, the architecture unites option-specific evidence routing, joint cross-field attention, and schema-bound scoring.

By freezing Qwen3.8-27B for Clef and Qwen3.5-9B for Clef-flash, we jointly optimized the routing head alongside rank-256 low-rank adapters. Our post-training utilizes label-smoothed cross-entropy for valid schema outputs paired with a Brier loss to refine probability calibration. This training leverages our own internal synthetic datasets permutating field orders, prompts, and schema structures. We also developed Reinforcement Learning for Calibrated Decisions (RLCD) to serve as a secondary optimization target, granting partial credit to adjacent ordinal choices, rewarding fully precise record outputs, and applying a reference penalty to prevent distribution shift, giving us better accuracy and generalization.

This means that we were able to achieve a few novel things with Clef: we improved accuracy of the model in classification, constrained it to output only probabilities instead of text generation, and made it faster than Jev and the base Qwen models.

How fine-tuning can extend the capabilities of Clef

We heard a lot of internal use cases that required fine-tuning our Clef model to be built into our agentic workflows at Cloudflare. For example, internal teams want a classifier model to be able to evaluate Trust & Safety submissions, help us triage Cloudflare Support requests, or even to be built-in to our Bot products to decide if a crawler is a good bot or bad bot.

These use cases are incredibly specific and we have had many years of labelled decisions that we could use to train a specific classifier. When you fine-tune a model, you may give up some general purpose performance in exchange for higher accuracy in a specific domain.. Because Cloudflare has more than 15 years of network data across different domains, we can fine-tune a model to fit these specific use cases which is more accurate and faster than our generic Clef model. We’re working with internal teams already to figure out how we can post-train Clef to create powerful ML models that boost our impact and improve workflows across Cloudflare. These internal teams and use cases are the next remit of our new FDE fine-tuning team and basis for our reinforcement learning (RL) product.

Our new RL service

We are offering a service to help customers fine-tune Clef to suit their workloads with our hands-on FDE team. From that, we’ll learn from our hands-on experiences to build a self-serve platform that customers can use to capture data, fine-tune, and redeploy the model, all on Cloudflare.

This has actually been a long time coming — we’ve been building our AI platform to have the right primitives where we could be building a custom RL product. The interest in Jev shows the need for a fast, small, specific, classifier model, and we chose this to be our niche to start experimenting with RL environments.

To do this, we leverage the primitives that we already have built on our Cloudflare platform:

  • Cloudflare AI Gateway – pass all your AI traffic through AI Gateway and automatically create a dataset of requests for your use case
  • Cloudflare Workers AI – generate rollouts against the base Clef model
  • Cloudflare Containers – RL sandbox for scoring and replaying agent actions
  • [NEW] Trainer – update weights of fine-tuned Clef model
  • Cloudflare Workers AI + BYO Model – redeploy the fine-tuned model on Workers AI

This combines a few work-in-progress pieces of the AI Platform that we’ve been working on, including AI Gateway that captures your AI traffic so you can leverage your own request/response data, Containers for RL Sandboxes, and Workers AI’s Bring Your Own Model (Cog) work that has been progressing since our acquisition of Replicate. 

Try it out today

We’re excited to launch our first Cloudflare-trained ML model from the Workers AI team today. We’re still early here and have a lot more improvements in store, but it is a wonderful first showcase of the hard work we’ve been doing on the AI Platform team. We believe that Clef has the ability to disrupt the way we use agents, which fits naturally into Cloudflare’s mission of being the agent cloud.

If you have specific use cases and are already customers of these products — we’d love to chat with you and be design partners as we experiment in this space.

Try out the Clef models hosted on Workers AI, download the weights on Hugging Face if you’d like to explore for yourself, and reach out if you have fine-tuning use cases you’d like us to help with.

Our ML team has been growing in impact, from model optimizations to model training research. If you’re interested in joining our mission, check out our open roles.

item.title: AI Search is now generally available
item.description: AI Search is now generally available. It embeds image pixels directly for visual search, runs optical character recognition on scanned PDFs, accepts files up to 10 MiB, and works with any chat model. Here's what's new and how pricing works.
item.dc:creator: Gabriel Massadas
Nelson Duarte
Ashish Vinodkumar
item.content:encoded:
Cloudflare’s AI Search combines Workers AI, Vectorize, R2, and Browser Run into a fully managed index and retrieval pipeline. Since we launched AI Search over a year ago, we’ve seen developers use it to power a wide range of search use cases, from searching internal documentation to powering search for their websites. We use AI Search ourselves to power search on our own blog and developer docs.

Starting today, AI Search is generally available. And as part of it, we've expanded and improved our support for multimodal formats beyond text, adding native image embeddings, optical character recognition (OCR) for PDFs, and support for larger files.

As part of general availability, we’ll start billing for AI Search on November 1, 2026, and continue to offer a generous free tier on all Workers plans.

New: multimodal embedding and retrieval

An image is more than the sentence used to describe it. Product texture, screenshot state, chart relationships, document layout, and fine visual detail can all disappear when pixels are compressed into a caption.

AI Search now preserves both signals: it embeds image pixels directly for visual retrieval while retaining captions for textual understanding. To keep these richer representations efficient, AI Search leverages Matryoshka Representation Learning (MRL), allowing smaller embeddings to retain useful information while keeping storage manageable and search fast.

Although we originally supported retrieval over images, the implementation was naive: we would perform object detection, generate a caption, and then embed that text. This made images searchable, but only through the details captured in the caption. Now, we do both — caption-based understanding and native image retrieval.

Native multimodal retrieval is available today with the Qwen3-VL-Embedding model. At query time, AI Search checks whether your instance’s embedding model supports images. If it does, a query image is embedded directly by that model, landing in the same vector space as your indexed images and text.

If your embedding model is text-only, you can still query with an image. AI Search converts the query image to text with ToMarkdown and searches using the resulting caption. This gives every model basic multimodal support, while models with native image support get the full visual signal.

Caption-based understanding

A small bird with black-and-white markings perched among golden fruit and green leaves

Native Image Retrieval

Can match details omitted from the caption: the geometry of the bird’s white eyebrow stripe, its yellow-green plumage, the mixture of smooth and weathered fruit, the leaves’ deeply ribbed texture, and the image’s warm palette and shallow-focus composition.

The caption is a compressed interpretation of the image. Capturing every potentially useful detail requires long or specialized captions, written with the eventual search query in mind. Native image embeddings preserve visual characteristics without requiring the caption to anticipate which details matter.

This enables searches that are difficult to express precisely with words. You can describe an image you want to find, provide another image to locate visually similar results, or combine both, such as “a bird with similar markings” or “a bird perched on a leafy branch with plums.” It is useful for product discovery, screenshot matching, charts, diagrams, scanned documents, and other collections where color, texture, composition, or spatial relationships matter.

Here’s how a query moves through AI Search. First, the query is optionally rewritten, then embedded (image queries are embedded directly by multimodal models, or captioned first by text-only models). Vector and keyword search run in parallel, and results are fused and optionally reranked. The top chunks are returned, or passed to a generation model to write an answer.

Bigger files and OCR for scanned documents

AI Search now accepts your text files (Markdown, HTML, CSV, JSON and similar) and PDFs up to 10 MiB, up from 4 MiB. Many PDFs are really scanned images with no extractable text. For those, turn on OCR and AI Search reads the text from each page before chunking and embedding it. OCR is available to every account and is billed under the new AI Search pricing as image processing ingestion tokens.

Now in GA: billing and pricing for AI Search

During our August 2026 Agents Week, we announced preview pricing for AI Search. With the product going GA today, we’re announcing billing for AI Search that is going live on November 1, 2026. We’ll send a reminder email before billing is enabled.

AI Search pricing is designed, so you can estimate your bill before you index a single file. You pay for three things: the content you ingest, the data you store, and the queries you run. The work in between (parsing, chunking, embedding with Workers AI models, keyword indexing, and reranking) is included. There are no instance hours, capacity units, or monthly minimums to size up front, and small projects fit inside the free monthly allotment.

Ingestion pricing is based on one rate per token with whichever Workers AI embedding model you pick, and tokens are counted the same way for every model. Switching from a text-only embedding model to a multimodal one doesn't change what you pay to ingest, unless you are also processing images (add-on fee). Storage is priced on the size of data in your indices. Querying is priced based on the type of query (semantic vs. full-text) and how many queries you send.

Estimating your cost comes down to how much content you index, how much you store, and how many queries you expect. Here's the pricing we announced in preview, with one tweak that we’re making: on the free monthly allotment, you will receive 1,000 semantic queries and 1,000 full-text queries (instead of a shared pool of 2,000 queries).

What’s next

Multimodal embedding support is just the first step; we’re building an ingestion pipeline to support full video and audio processing to allow our customers to search their rich media assets.

We’re also refactoring the keyword search engine so that it scales better with your content requirements, particularly for when you have big data stores where the current implementation has limits.

Finally, we’re developing better and simpler ways to enable AI Search and create indexes for websites already running on Cloudflare. This ensures AI agents can discover, explore, and consume content more easily and efficiently.

Stay tuned for these follow-up announcements and more.
